claims.claim: FlashAttention is an exact attention algorithm that uses tiling to reduce HBM–SRAM reads and writes.
claims.label: supported

claims.claim: It processes blocks, computes softmax incrementally, recomputes attention on-chip in the backward pass, and fuses everything into one CUDA kernel.
claims.label: supported

claims.claim: It does more FLOPs because of recomputation but is faster from fewer HBM accesses; HBM accesses are the main factor in attention runtime; most Transformer ops are memory-bound.
claims.label: partial

claims.claim: Each new attention variant needs a new CUDA kernel, and implementations 'may also not be transferrable across GPU architectures.'
claims.label: unsupported

claims.claim: Beyond about 1K tokens some approximate methods such as Linformer become faster; past block size 256, runtime is limited by arithmetic and other factors.
claims.label: partial

claims.claim: FlashAttention-1 reached 25–40% of peak FLOPs/s; FlashAttention-2 reached 50–73% on A100; a 2–4x figure versus optimized baselines.
claims.label: supported

claims.claim: FlashAttention-2 reached only 35% utilization on H100; FlashAttention-3 reached about 75% in FP16 using Hopper-specific features.
claims.label: supported

claims.claim: 15% end-to-end speedup on BERT-large (seq 512) versus the MLPerf 1.1 record; 3x on GPT-2 (seq 1K).
claims.label: supported

sibyl.notes: Most claims trace to the excerpts. The quoted line about non-transferability across GPU architectures and the block-size-256 claim are not in the bounded excerpt. Sources are three primary papers from overlapping authors, and the answer explicitly says there is no independent source. Limitations are disclosed; the Linformer comparison is the only substantive narrowing evidence. The uncited claim is the statement that 'exact' means mathematically equivalent rather than bitwise identical.

claims.claim: FlashAttention is an 'IO-aware exact attention algorithm' that reduces HBM–SRAM reads and writes by tiling and computes the same output, not an approximation.
claims.label: supported

claims.claim: Softmax stays exact through a running row max and normalizer with exponential rescaling; Theorem 1 says the algorithm returns softmax(QK^T)V with O(N) extra memory.
claims.label: partial

claims.claim: The backward pass stores the output and softmax statistics and recomputes attention on-chip; extra FLOPs are outweighed by lower memory traffic.
claims.label: supported

claims.claim: HBM accesses fall from Θ(Nd+N^2) to Θ(N^2 d^2/M), up to 9x fewer, with a lower bound that no exact algorithm can asymptotically beat across SRAM sizes.
claims.label: supported

claims.claim: 15% on BERT-large vs MLPerf 1.1, 3x on GPT-2 (1K), 2.4x on LRA; 0.7 perplexity gain and Path-X/Path-256 results from longer context.
claims.label: supported

claims.claim: FA1 reached 25–40% of peak because of poor work partitioning; FA2 is about 2x faster at 50–73% of peak on A100.
claims.label: supported

claims.claim: FA3 uses Hopper-specific asynchrony, TMA, warp specialization and FP8; 1.5–2.0x over FA2 on H100, 740 TFLOPs/s (75%); FP8 has 2.6x lower error than a baseline FP8 attention, so it is not error-free.
claims.label: supported

claims.claim: Implementations 'may not be transferrable across GPU architectures' and each variant needs its own CUDA kernel; the IO-optimality proof is single-GPU, with multi-GPU left as future work.
claims.label: unsupported

native.notes: Well grounded in the abstracts and introduction. The Theorem 1 details, the running-max rescaling details, the transferability quote and the single-GPU scope are not in the bounded excerpt. The answer discloses that it skipped most of the paper and has no independent replication. The FP8 error and kernel-version-dependence points narrow the conclusion modestly.

claims.claim: HBM accesses fall from Θ(Nd+N^2) to Θ(N^2 d^2/M), with a lower bound that no exact algorithm can asymptotically beat over a range of SRAM sizes.
claims.label: supported

claims.claim: Figure 2 shows 40.3 GB vs 4.4 GB of HBM reads/writes and 41.7 ms vs 7.3 ms runtime.
claims.label: unsupported

claims.claim: Original paper gains: BERT-large ~15% vs MLPerf 1.1, GPT-2 up to 3x vs HuggingFace, LRA 2.4x, attention 7.6x, memory up to 20x lower.
claims.label: partial

claims.claim: FA3 forward pass is 1.5–2.0x faster than FA2 on H100, up to 740 TFLOPs/s (~75%); FA2 reached ~35% on H100; gains rely on Hopper features, though the authors say the techniques should transfer to other accelerators.
claims.label: supported

claims.claim: FA3's FP8 kernel is not persistent, trails cuDNN at small sequence lengths and with causal masking, and is roughly at par at head dims 128/256 without causal masking.
claims.label: partial

claims.claim: Each new attention variant needs a hand-written CUDA kernel and may not transfer across GPU architectures; optimality is shown only for a single GPU.
claims.label: unsupported

claims.claim: GPT-2 speedup is 3x vs HuggingFace but only about 1.7–1.8x vs Megatron-LM.
claims.label: unsupported

claims.claim: A secondary blog claims standard attention can match FlashAttention-2 below about 256 tokens.
claims.label: unsupported

deep_research.notes: Several specific quantitative claims are not in the bounded excerpts: the Figure 2 numbers, the Megatron 1.7–1.8x figure (the excerpt says 3x vs both HuggingFace and Megatron-LM), the FA3 FP16 RMSE values (the excerpt states only same error as FA2 and better than standard), the 20x memory figure, and Theorem 1. The blog does not contain the 256-token claim. The KV-cache decoding claim is also not in the blog, although the claim that compute-bound prefill sees smaller gains is. The repo memory-bandwidth claim has no URL. Strengths: the cuDNN footnote and the baseline-dependence point substantively narrow the gains, and secondary-source claims are flagged as unverified.
